{{Short description|Set of three congruent geometrical helices with the same axis}}
{{About|the biophysical phenomenon|the management concept|triple helix model of innovation|the album by Anat Cohen Tentet|Triple Helix (album)}}
[[File:Collagen (triple helix protein).jpg|alt=a molecular model of the collagen triple helix|thumb|The collagen triple helix is a triple helix formed from three separate protein helices, spiraling around the same axis.]]
In the fields of [[geometry]] and [[biochemistry]], a '''triple helix''' ({{plural form}}: '''triple helices''') is a set of three congruent geometrical [[Helix|helices]] with the same [[Coordinate axis|axis]], differing by a [[Translation (geometry)|translation]] along the axis. This means that each of the helices keeps the same distance from the central axis. As with a single helix, a triple helix may be characterized by its pitch, diameter, and handedness. Examples of triple helices include [[Triple-stranded DNA|triplex DNA]],<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Bernués J, Azorín F | chapter = Triple-Stranded DNA | title = Nucleic Acids and Molecular Biology | volume = 9 | date = 1995 | pages = 1–21 | publisher = Springer | location = Berlin, Heidelberg | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-79488-9_1 | isbn = 978-3-642-79490-2 }}</ref> triplex [[RNA]],<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Buske FA, Mattick JS, Bailey TL | title = Potential in vivo roles of nucleic acid triple-helices | journal = RNA Biology | volume = 8 | issue = 3 | pages = 427–439 | date = May 2011 | pmid = 21525785 | pmc = 3218511 | doi = 10.4161/rna.8.3.14999 }}</ref> the [[collagen helix]],<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4jH_SuLShWcC&pg=PA7|title=Collagen: Primer in Structure, Processing and Assembly| vauthors = Bächinger HP |date=2005-05-03|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-23272-8}}</ref> and collagen-like [[protein]]s.

== Structure ==
A triple helix is named such because it is made up of three separate [[Helix|helices]].  Each of these helices shares the same axis, but they do not take up the same space because each helix is translated angularly around the axis.  Generally, the identity of a triple helix depends on the type of helices that make it up.  For example: a triple helix made of three strands of collagen protein is a collagen triple helix, and a triple helix made of three strands of [[DNA]] is a DNA triple helix.

As with other types of helices, triple helices have handedness: right-handed or left-handed.  A right-handed helix moves around its axis in a clockwise direction from beginning to end. A left-handed helix is the right-handed helix's mirror image, and it moves around the axis in a counterclockwise direction from beginning to end.<ref name="Kuriyan_2012">{{Cite book |title=The molecules of life: physical and chemical principles| vauthors = Kuriyan J, Konforti B, Wemmer D |isbn=978-0-8153-4188-8|location=New York | publisher = Garland Science, Taylor & Francis Group |oclc=779577263|date=2012-07-25}}</ref>  The beginning and end of a helical molecule are defined based on certain markers in the molecule that do not change easily.  For example: the beginning of a helical protein is its [[N-terminus|N terminus]], and the beginning of a single strand of DNA is its [[5' end]].<ref name="Kuriyan_2012" />

The [[collagen]] triple helix is made of three collagen peptides, each of which forms its own left-handed polyproline helix.<ref name="Shoulders_2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Shoulders MD, Raines RT | title = Collagen structure and stability | journal = Annual Review of Biochemistry | volume = 78 | pages = 929–958 | date = 2009 | pmid = 19344236 | pmc = 2846778 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.biochem.77.032207.120833 }}</ref> When the three chains combine, the triple helix adopts a right-handed orientation. The collagen peptide is composed of repeats of [[Glycine|Gly]]-X-Y, with the second residue (X) usually being [[Proline|Pro]] and the third (Y) being hydroxyproline.<ref name="Fidler_2018">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fidler AL, Boudko SP, Rokas A, Hudson BG | title = The triple helix of collagens - an ancient protein structure that enabled animal multicellularity and tissue evolution | journal = Journal of Cell Science | volume = 131 | issue = 7 | pages = jcs203950 | date = April 2018 | pmid = 29632050 | pmc = 5963836 | doi = 10.1242/jcs.203950 }}</ref><ref name="Shoulders_2009" />

A DNA triple helix is made up of three separate DNA strands, each oriented with the sugar/phosphate backbone on the outside of the helix and the bases on the inside of the helix.  The bases are the part of the molecule closest to the triple helix's axis, and the backbone is the part of the molecule farthest away from the axis.  The third strand occupies the major groove of relatively normal duplex DNA.<ref name="Jain_2008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Jain A, Wang G, Vasquez KM | title = DNA triple helices: biological consequences and therapeutic potential | journal = Biochimie | volume = 90 | issue = 8 | pages = 1117–1130 | date = August 2008 | pmid = 18331847 | pmc = 2586808 | doi = 10.1016/j.biochi.2008.02.011 }}</ref>  The bases in triplex DNA are arranged to match up according to a [[Hoogsteen base pair|Hoogsteen]] base pairing scheme.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Duca M, Vekhoff P, Oussedik K, Halby L, Arimondo PB | title = The triple helix: 50 years later, the outcome | journal = Nucleic Acids Research | volume = 36 | issue = 16 | pages = 5123–5138 | date = September 2008 | pmid = 18676453 | pmc = 2532714 | doi = 10.1093/nar/gkn493 }}</ref> Similarly, RNA triple helices are formed as a result of a single stranded RNA forming hydrogen bonds with an RNA duplex; the duplex consists of Watson-Crick base pairing while the third strand binds via Hoogsteen base pairing.<ref name="Conrad_2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Conrad NK | title = The emerging role of triple helices in RNA biology | journal = Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews. RNA | volume = 5 | issue = 1 | pages = 15–29 | date = 2014 | pmid = 24115594 | pmc = 4721660 | doi = 10.1002/wrna.1194 }}</ref>

== Stabilizing factors ==
The collagen triple helix has several characteristics that increase its stability.  When proline is incorporated into the Y position of the Gly-X-Y sequence, it is [[Post-translational modification|post-translationally modified]] to [[hydroxyproline]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brodsky B, Persikov AV | title = Molecular structure of the collagen triple helix | journal = Advances in Protein Chemistry | volume = 70 | pages = 301–339 | date = 2005-01-01 | pmid = 15837519 | doi = 10.1016/S0065-3233(05)70009-7 | isbn = 978-0-12-034270-9 | s2cid = 20879450 }}</ref>  The hydroxyproline can enter into favorable interactions with water, which stabilizes the triple helix because the Y residues are solvent-accessible in the triple helix structure. The individual helices are also held together by an extensive network of amide-amide hydrogen bonds formed between the strands, each of which contributes approximately -2 kcal/mol to the overall free energy of the triple helix.<ref name="Shoulders_2009" /> The formation of the superhelix not only protects the critical glycine residues on the interior of the helix, but also protects the overall protein from proteolysis.<ref name="Fidler_2018" />

Triple helix DNA and RNA are stabilized by many of the same forces that stabilize double-stranded DNA helices.  With nucleotide bases oriented to the inside of the helix, closer to its axis, bases engage in hydrogen bonding with other bases.  The bonded bases in the center exclude water, so the [[hydrophobic effect]] is particularly important in the stabilization of DNA triple helices.<ref name="Kuriyan_2012" />

== Biological role ==

=== Proteins ===
Members of the collagen superfamily are major contributors to the extracellular matrix. The triple helical structure provides strength and stability to collagen fibers by providing great resistance to tensile stress. The rigidity of the collagen fibers is an important factor that can withstand most mechanical stress, making it an ideal protein for macromolecular transport and overall structural support throughout the body.<ref name="Fidler_2018" />

=== DNA ===
There are some oligonucleotide sequences, called triplet-forming [[oligonucleotide]]s (TFOs) that can bind to form a triplex with a longer molecule of double-stranded DNA; TFOs can inactivate a gene or help to induce mutations.<ref name="Jain_2008" /> TFOs can only bind to certain sites in a larger molecule, so researchers must first determine whether a TFO can bind to the gene of interest. [[Twisted intercalating nucleic acid]] is sometimes used to improve this process. Mapping of genome-wide TFO-TTS pairs by sequencing is a useful way to study the triplex forming DNA in the whole genome using oligo-library. 

=== RNA ===
In recent years, the biological function of triplex RNA has become more studied. Some roles include increasing stability, translation, influencing ligand binding, and catalysis. One example of ligand binding being influenced by a triple helix is in the SAM-II [[riboswitch]] where the triple helix creates a binding site that will uniquely accept ''S''-adenosylmethionine ([[S-Adenosyl methionine|SAM]]).<ref name="Conrad_2014" /> The ribonucleoprotein complex [[telomerase]], responsible for replicating the tail-ends of DNA ([[telomere]]s) also contains triplex RNA believed to be necessary for proper telomerase functioning.<ref name="Conrad_2014" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Theimer CA, Blois CA, Feigon J | title = Structure of the human telomerase RNA pseudoknot reveals conserved tertiary interactions essential for function | journal = Molecular Cell | volume = 17 | issue = 5 | pages = 671–682 | date = March 2005 | pmid = 15749017 | doi = 10.1016/j.molcel.2005.01.017 | doi-access = free }}</ref> The triple helix at the 3' end of the PAN and [[MALAT1]] long-noncoding RNAs serves to stabilize the RNA by protecting the Poly(A) tail from deadenylation, which subsequently affect their functions in viral pathogenesis and multiple human cancers.<ref name="Conrad_2014" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brown JA, Bulkley D, Wang J, Valenstein ML, Yario TA, Steitz TA, Steitz JA | title = Structural insights into the stabilization of MALAT1 noncoding RNA by a bipartite triple helix | journal = Nature Structural & Molecular Biology | volume = 21 | issue = 7 | pages = 633–640 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 24952594 | pmc = 4096706 | doi = 10.1038/nsmb.2844 }}</ref> Additionally, RNA triple helices can stabilize mRNAs by formation of a poly(A) tail 3'-end binding pocket.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Torabi SF, Vaidya AT, Tycowski KT, DeGregorio SJ, Wang J, Shu MD, Steitz TA, Steitz JA | display-authors = 6 | title = RNA stabilization by a poly(A) tail 3'-end binding pocket and other modes of poly(A)-RNA interaction | journal = Science | volume = 371 | issue = 6529 | article-number = eabe6523 | date = February 2021 | pmid = 33414189 | pmc = 9491362 | doi = 10.1126/science.abe6523 | s2cid = 231195473 }}</ref>

== Computational Tools ==

=== TDF (Triplex Domain Finder) ===
TDF is a [[Python (programming language)|Python]]-based package <ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kuo CC, Hänzelmann S, Sentürk Cetin N, Frank S, Zajzon B, Derks JP, Akhade VS, Ahuja G, Kanduri C, Grummt I, Kurian L, Costa IG | display-authors = 6 | title = Detection of RNA-DNA binding sites in long noncoding RNAs | journal = Nucleic Acids Research | volume = 47 | issue = 6 | pages = e32 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 30698727 | doi = 10.1093/nar/gkz037 | pmc = 6451187 }}</ref> to predict RNA-DNA triplex formation potential. The software starts by enumerating the substrings between TFO and TTS and uses statistical tests to find out significant result compared to the background.

=== Triplexfpp ===
Triplexfpp<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhang Y, Long Y, Kwoh CK | title = Deep learning based DNA:RNA triplex forming potential prediction | journal = BMC Bioinformatics | volume = 21 | issue = 1 | page = 522 | date = November 2020 | pmid = 33183242 | pmc = 7663897 | doi = 10.1186/s12859-020-03864-0 | doi-access = free }}</ref> is based on deep learning methods. This Python-based pipeline can help predict the most likely triplex-forming lncRNA. However since the lncRNA for training is limited, there is a long way to go before machine learning and deep learning methods can be applied.
